cards.question: Define the hot zone.
cards.answer: Area of immediate danger (contamination, fire, collapse, active violence) — entry only by properly protected specialist teams.

cards.question: What happens in the warm zone?
cards.answer: Decontamination corridor, casualty collection points, rapid lifesaving care under protection/escort.

cards.question: What belongs in the cold zone?
cards.answer: Command post, treatment area, loading zone, staging, rehab, media area, morgue (out of view).

cards.question: Ideal treatment area location?
cards.answer: Cold zone, upwind/uphill, flat, lit, sheltered, room to expand, next to the loading zone, one way in/one way out.

cards.question: Which treatment section sits nearest the loading zone exit?
Ideal staging area?
cards.answer: On the approach route, out of sight of the hazard, safe, with room to park in rows and a one-way path to the loading zone.

cards.question: Where should the helicopter LZ be?
cards.answer: Cold zone, clear of wires/obstacles/debris, away from the treatment area because of rotor wash; typically ~100 × 100 ft (≈30 × 30 m) — follow your air provider.

cards.question: Where is the morgue placed?
cards.answer: Cold zone, secure, out of public and patient view.

cards.question: Rule for positioning near HazMat?
cards.answer: Upwind, uphill, upstream; use the ERG for isolation and protective action distances.

cards.question: Approximate stand-off for a pipe bomb?
cards.answer: ≈70 ft mandatory evacuation; ≈1,200 ft outdoor preferred evacuation (DHS/NCTC chart).

cards.question: What is a Casualty Collection Point (CCP)?
cards.answer: A point (often in the warm zone) where casualties are gathered for triage and rapid care before movement to the treatment area.

cards.question: Why one-way patient and vehicle flow?
cards.answer: Prevents congestion, collisions, and lost patients; ambulances never back through the scene.
